utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Milan Simic, Miroslav Tadic and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, the Prosecution is continuing with examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Philip Weiner for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dagovic.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, you were telling us about the day of the attack and how, during the morning hours, you had breakfast with the Bicics, how you started to work in the cellar to build some sort of bomb shelter or so. Now, during that late morning, did you see Hasan Bicic?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see Hasan later, or rather I saw him after breakfast, when we went to check whether everything was all right with the pizzeria, or rather his shop.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Tell us what you and Hasan did. Tell the Court.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We unlocked the shop, we checked to see whether everything was all right, we closed some window that we usually leave open during the night in order to get some fresh air in, we realised that we could not work that day, and we locked up the shop, and we each went our own ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When you walked to the shop, and then I assume walked home, were you carrying a gun?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What kind of gun were you carrying?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a pistol, which I carried with me every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Why did you carry a pistol with you every day?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had a permit for it, and often I carried a lot of money with me, or rather the earnings from several of Mr. Hasan Bicic's shops and cafes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So it was nothing unusual for you to be carrying a gun on that day?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I used to carry that on the previous day and every other day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, while you were out walking to and from the pizzeria, did you see anything?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw vehicles of the former Yugoslav People's Army moving in all directions, and I saw -- somewhere in the direction of the department store or perhaps a bit further off, I saw soldiers moving about in camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you said you returned home.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, what did you do when you got back home?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What did I do? I talked to my parents. I told them what I saw, and as I said, I was home.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, did you listen to the radio at all?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the only station that we managed to hear, because we did not dare listen to any other stations, in fear of the then authorities. We listened to Radio Bosanski Samac, or rather -- Bosanski Samac, the name of Bosanski Samac, was changed into Serb Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did they change the name of the radio station?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The station that was called Radio Bosanski Samac was from then on called Radio Srpski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what did you hear on the radio station?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we heard that, as they called them, the Serb authorities had taken over the town of Samac, that everything was all right. They were calling upon people to surrender their weapons, or rather, to take them out in front of their houses, so that they, or rather, the soldiers of the 4th Detachment and of the Yugoslav People's Army, then the Serb army, could collect these weapons with their trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, when you said they were telling people to turn over their weapons, was this one single broadcast or was this several broadcasts?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They said that on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, did anyone ever come for your weapon, your pistol?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And could you tell the Court about that situation.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a new thing for me. To me it looked like a war movie. A tank was moving along the street, and Mr. Simo Zaric and Mr. Miroslav Tadic were standing on this tank, and they were saying where the tank should stop, in front of which house. And then the drivers of the tank would point the barrel at that house and all the soldiers who were walking by the tank would, on the orders given by Mr. Zaric, enter the yards, or rather, our houses, and they asked for weapons by force, or rather, they used all kinds of words. I mean, I don't know how to put this. It looked like a command, orders. They would say, "Surrender your weapons." They would surround the house, the yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Just let's take it one step at a time. Did they stop at your house?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Where were you when they stopped at your home?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment I was in the yard of my house, so I could see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when they stopped in front of your house, who was present?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Among the soldiers. Did you see any of the defendants present in front of your house?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw Mr. Simo Zaric and Mr. Miroslav Tadic, in addition to the other soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And about how many soldiers were there?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in my estimate, perhaps over 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And just tell us, from what you saw, exactly what happened, as best as you can remember, when they stopped in front of your house.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What happened? Well, on Mr. Zaric's orders, they entered my yard and they were asking for weapons, or rather, they were screaming. They were yelling in the yard, "Surrender your weapons. Get out." And I said that I was in the yard, and at that moment I was moving into the house. And they got in there. My mother, my father, and my brother went out. They went to the steps of our house. And they pointed guns at us and they asked us to hand over our weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what did you do?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since we were civilians, I was afraid that something could happen, and I had hidden that pistol in the cellar of my house. Escorted by a soldier, Goran Buzakovic, I entered my cellar and I surrendered this pistol to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And this Goran Buzakovic, what military unit was he from?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was from the unit of Mr. Simo Zaric, or rather, the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And these other soldiers that were there, where were they from? What unit, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew most of the soldiers. They belonged to the 4th Detachment. But there were others I did not know. I don't know whether they were the so-called members of the special forces from Serbia or whether they were the members of the 4th Detachment from other villages, but they were unknown to me, at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, after you handed him your pistol, did they ask you for any other weapons, or did they search, or what did they do? Tell the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were looking for hand grenades, automatic rifles, which I did not have, and they partly searched the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did they eventually leave?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what did they do next, if you saw?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would go to the next Bosnian Muslim houses, or rather, Bosnian Catholic houses belonging to Croats, and they were looking for weapons there too as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you notice whether they stopped at any of the Serbian homes?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you -- when you say "no," do you mean you didn't notice or they didn't stop at any Serbian homes?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they did not stop, because they didn't need to. They were in their units for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, when you talked about the 4th Detachment, are you -- were you familiar with the 4th Detachment prior to this attack?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And who was in charge of the 4th Detachment, as best you knew?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, and Mr. Miroslav Tadic was his right hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And who was out enlisting members for the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Simo Zaric and, as I said, his right hand, Mr. Miroslav Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, do you know where the meetings for the 4th Detachment were being held prior to the attack, in the months prior to the attack?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Where was that?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the cafe of Mr. Miroslav Tadic, which was called AS.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And was this common knowledge in Bosanski Samac, that the meetings were being held there for the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was a sort of secret that everybody knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, after you turned over your weapon, during the day, did you hear any other broadcasts during these first few days of the attack?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. During these first few days, I heard over the radio that all the citizens of Bosnian or Croat, or rather Muslim or Croat ethnicity, should report at the building of the Territorial Defence, or rather the former Yugoslav People's Army, that is to say everyone from the ages of 16 to 60. And we were ordered to wear on our left arm white armbands so that they could recognise us even better.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When you say "we were ordered," what do you mean? Who had to wear those white armbands on their left arm?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did they state on that -- during that radio broadcast what would happen if you didn't report to the TO?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They said that they would be shot, executed, whoever would not report to the Territorial Defence building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: During those broadcasts, was there any information about public meetings by Muslims or Croatians?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They said that they should not assemble in groups bigger than three persons, and this related only to the Muslims and the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, over those next few days, did you see any signs or posters or announcements concerning any of these orders that you heard over Radio Serbia or Radio Serbia Samac?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were posters that were all over town, and it said on them that no more than three Croats or three Muslims respectively were allowed to assemble.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was there any signature on those announcements or posters?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I can remember, the signature of Stevan Todorovic, nicknamed Stiv.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, as a result of that order, what did you do? Did you go to the TO?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I was afraid for my life. I was so young, I was only 22 years old. I wanted to live my life, so I did report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And who did you go with?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went with my brother and with a few young men, Muslims and Croats from my street.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How were you dressed when you went there? Did you wear the -- basically, did you wear the armband?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the armband. We didn't dare go out without an armband. So I did have this armband on my left arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when you were walking there, or to or from the Territorial Defence building, did you see any other Muslims or Croatians along the streets?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were going in the same direction as I was, because I saw them at the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And were they wearing those armbands?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What about the Serbs? Did you see any Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And were they wearing armbands, too?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They differed from us only by virtue of the fact that they were wearing uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Once you got to the TO, what happened? What did they do?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't understand this. When I got to the TO?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the Territorial Defence building. They told you to report to the Territorial Defence building. What did they do with you at the Territorial Defence building?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They wrote down our names, or rather we reported there. We had to bring our personal IDs. We gave them to them, and then they recorded us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, while you were at the Territorial Defence building, where is the police station or the SUP in relation to the Territorial Defence building?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This building is across the street, that is to say opposite the Territorial Defence building. And if I may say something, what I really remember is the screams that could be heard there. They were beating people, and these people were moaning and screaming and crying from the pain inflicted on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you could hear that across the street at the Territorial Defence building?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because the prisoners were in the same building, in the building of the former police station in Samac. I could see soldiers in camouflage uniforms that were going in and out of the police building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of these soldiers as being local people?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, they were the so-called members of the specialist forces, or rather soldiers from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, at that point, you've registered, you hear screaming from the building. How do you feel?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, I was wondering whether they had brought us to this building on purpose so that we would hear these screams and that they could intimidate us in this way. So I felt as if I were drifting in the air. I don't know whether it was out of fear or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you do anything else at the Territorial Defence building?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did they ask you -- did they try and recruit you, try and mobilise you into the JNA? Did they ask you about forced labour at that point, or anything else at that point?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They offered us weapons, or rather, to join the army of Republika Srpska, which I and most of the other people refused, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did you do next?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then I went to my home.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us about the forced labour? What happens next with regard to forced labour? How did you know where to go to work?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew because a messenger would come to the house and say that I had to report immediately at the local commune building. We would go there and then they would assign us for labour, forced labour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, in relation to your visit to the Territorial Defence building and your return home, how soon after your return home did one of these couriers or messengers arrive?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly, but I think it was on the following day, or one of the following days.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, they told you to go to a certain location?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did you see other people at that location who had to do forced labour?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And was this just the men that had to do the forced labour?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I noticed was that it was only Muslims and Croats, and there were old people, women, and even children, say, 15 or 16 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Who in your family had to do the forced labour?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my family, everybody had to do forced labour. To tell you quite frankly, my parents worked much less than my brother and I did, and we were exposed to very hard labour, my brother and I.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: During your forced labour assignments, give me the age of the oldest -- a range of the oldest people and the youngest people.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said, they were like between 16 and 60. They asked for all these people to report to them. So it was between the ages of 16 and 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were there any Serbs that had to work forced labour?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How often did you have to work or were you forced to work?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went every day, and the work would go on for about 10 or 12 hours a day even.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did have you to work on the weekends, on Saturdays and Sundays, too?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sometimes even during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you fed?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you paid for this work?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What about the sick, the sick people, or people who weren't feeling well? Did they have to work?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What about the leaders, the SDA leaders, or the leaders of the different political parties, the educated, highly educated people? Did they have to work?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What sort of jobs were they given?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one occasion, or rather, while I was working in town, since he had already been arrested, Mr. Sulejman Tihic had to sweep the street in front of the police building. Now, what did I notice? They were laughing at him and they were humiliating him, because he was a man who held a high position, who was educated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What sort of jobs were you assigned?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most often we dug trenches, but we did other work, too, in addition to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Tell the Tribunal the different types of work that you did, please.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We dug trenches, we carried sacks, bags of sand, very heavy bags, maybe 50 kilos in weight, and we took them to the silo so that they could make shelters or shields. And then from the silo buildings you could see far into Croatia, and probably shoot -- the snipers would shoot somebody on the other side of the river Sava.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was there ever any gunfire while you were working on these trenches or silos?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was on the embankment, actually, on the border with village Prud. There was shooting, and I noticed that each time the shooting was caused by the soldiers of the army of Republika Srpska, who provoked by firing on the Croatian side, so that they would fire back, and we were in between. They didn't even allow us to take shelter when there was shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did women have to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see women digging trenches, but they did perform other work.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What type of work did the women do?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly, they swept the streets. They even used to clean the houses or the apartments which were taken by the Serbs there at that time from the special forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, at no time do they ever feed you during this forced labour, during these forced labour assignments?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever ask for food or water?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Tell us -- tell the Court what happened when you asked for food or water.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At one time I was hit in the head with a pistol instead of being given a piece of bread.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Who struck you with the pistol?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the soldier who hit me with the pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, were there soldiers supervising this work at these sites?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And who gave the orders at these sites, the soldiers, these guards, or who?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly at these places, there were soldiers from the 4th Detachment who were under the command of, as I've already said, of Mr. Simo Zaric, and I mostly knew those guys.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you see other soldiers from -- who you referred to as specials or paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And how were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They wore camouflage uniforms. They had more modern weapons. For example, the Grey Wolves, they carried hats which were like cowboy hats. They also had paint on their faces. Compared to the soldiers of -- who were part of Arkan's Tigers, who wore woolen caps which you could pull down over your head and face so that only the eyes were visible and there was also an opening for the mouth. And of course, both of them had their own insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, when you worked these jobs, did you strictly work in the town of Samac, or did you work in other towns or in other municipalities?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I was imprisoned, I worked at Samac -- in Samac and also in the villages around Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How did you get to these jobs? Did you have to go yourself to the village, or did someone take you, or what was the process?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, before the local commune where we would gather, a truck would arrive there, and we had to get into that truck, and then they would transport us to the forced labour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever speak to any of these paramilitaries during the forced labour or while -- or during your later detention?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did they tell you why they came to Samac?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They had a Serbian accent which I was very familiar with, and they would say, "We've been called to come here. We've been brought here in order to save the Serbs who are being killed by the Muslims and the Croats." But as they themselves said, this wasn't true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did any of them ever indicate that they had any sort of criminal background?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Tell the Court what they said.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly they spoke amongst themselves, and sometimes they would look directly at us and talk, and this would refer to us, that these were mostly prisoners, criminals, whom the Serbian authorities had released, not all of them, but most of them had released from prisons and told them to go to Bosnia to fight, and that's why they were released. And they told them everything that they looted and plundered was theirs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's continue on to the end of April, 1992. Do you know a soldier by the -- that uses the nickname of Tralja?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see him with Hasan Bicic?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Tell the Court about that incident, please.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hasan Bicic was brought by two soldiers, one of whom was the person called Tralja. They were brought to my house. Hasan was in a very bad state. He was beaten, bloodied. I think he had a broken nose. He was very filthy. He had a long -- longer beard. And this is not how I knew him. He asked for money. Actually, these Serb special forces asked for money so that they could pay for the head of the brother of Hasan Bicic, Muhamed Bicic, so that they wouldn't kill him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave them 800 German marks right away, and I told them I didn't have any more. I did have more, but I didn't give everything because I was afraid that they would take everything. I told them that I would collect the money and that then I would give it to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did they leave after that?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did he ever return, this Tralja, for more money or other items?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What happened when he returned?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can go back to the previous question --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- if you permit me? On that occasion, when Tralja was together with Hasan Bicic, he ordered Hasan Bicic to take off a gold chain from my brother's neck. And Hasan personally took it, and he had to give it to Tralja, and then they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, when they came back, tell the Court what happened.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they came back, I had to give them the keys to my car, together with all the documents, all the car documents, the insurance, the travels -- the road licence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Why did you have to give them your vehicle?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because he had an automatic pistol pointed at my head and he was very savage. There were blows and all the other things that went along with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, when you say "he," was that Tralja?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did this happen at your parents' home?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What was your vehicle worth?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I paid 7.300 German marks for my car. That vehicle was worth more at that time, but since I had bought it from the owner of the pizzeria where I worked, from Hasan Bicic, I got a much better price for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did they take anything else from your home on that occasion, or from your parents' home?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did they take?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was gold jewellery, money, and small items which were of some value.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What ever happened to Hasan's jeep that he was letting you use, Hasan Bicic's jeep?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I put Hasan's jeep in the garage, but they drove that jeep off as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Who was "they" who drove it off?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serb specials.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, were you ever given a receipt or a certificate for any of the jewellery, the vehicles, any of the items that were taken?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we never received any written receipts. We only received blows as a form of receipt.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Obviously, you weren't paid for these items.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: By the way, did you ever see Hasan's jeep again?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Tell the Court how you saw the jeep and in what circumstances.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was when I was already detained in the police building. A member of the Serb special forces came, Slobodan Miljkovic, called Lugar, and he asked for me, since he had heard - who else could he have heard it from but from local Serbs - that I drove the jeep around. So he was asking for me so that I could show him how he could take the jeep out of the towing position, because when the jeep was in that position, it could go, but it couldn't go very fast. So that I then had to get out of the camp to show him how to do that. He probably wasn't a very good driver, because a good driver would know himself how you could do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let us go down another week, to May 5th, approximately noontime. Could you tell us where you were?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On May 5th, in the morning, I was doing forced labour. Then I came home. A police vehicle came, and soldiers and policemen came out of the car. They entered my house. They searched my house. They took some small items with them. And since I was -- I often went hunting with my uncle, who later was killed in the camp, so we used to go hunting for game. And they took away binoculars. They took that with them. They confiscated that. They also took some silver glasses and some other things that I had, and they told me that I had to go for an informative talk at the police building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did they bring you to the police station for an informative talk?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when you say "the police station," where was that located?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the main street of our town, Marsala Tita street. They've changed its name now. It now has the name of some famous Serbian person. So that's where they took me. But this was no longer a real police station. It was a camp now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You mean a prison camp?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you enter the station?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Tell the Tribunal what happened once you went to the station.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I entered the police station, I was brutally beaten in the hall of the station, of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stevan Todorovic was there, amongst others.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And tell them what he did.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First they took the rest of the gold that -- gold jewellery that I was wearing. They beat me. Stevan asked me where my money and my car were. They laughed at me, they spat at me, they beat me all over my body. I was in a very, very bad state. I was bleeding.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did they use to beat you with?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They beat me with everything. Mostly they beat me with batons, with their feet, anything that they could get their hands on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How long did this beating last?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my estimate, it lasted about 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what did they do with the property that they stole from you, the gold chains?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They gave them to Stevan Todorovic, those soldiers who were with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was it just gold chains that they robbed from you?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also had two bracelets, besides the chains; I also had some rings. They took all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And was that all given to Stevan Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I was able to see, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What happened after you were beaten?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After they beat me - excuse me - they placed me in a room in the SUP building and they told me that they would come to interrogate me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you describe this room and what was in it or who was in it when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The room, if you look at it from the entrance to the building, it was on the right side, behind the reception. It used to be an office. At that time, in that room, there was one man, and that's where we waited for the interrogation. Soon after that, I was moved to a different room.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How many other people were in that room?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the other room there were about 13 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of those 13 people?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Where were they from?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were mostly people from villages, and there were also a couple of people from Samac amongst them, also including Esad Mesic. I also noticed a man from the municipality of Odzak, from Odzak. He was a taxi driver, and he was wounded in both shoulders by Serbian soldiers, and he told me at that time that they were forcing him to confess something which he didn't do and that they took his car, his taxi, that he intended to drive in the direction of Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How did the rest of the people appear?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They looked pretty terrible. They were badly beaten, bloodied. They had blood all over their trousers, their T-shirts. They had dried blood on their wounds. They were starving and they were pretty exhausted and tortured.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: These beaten people, were they soldiers? Were they wearing uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: From what ethnic groups were they, the ones you knew?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exclusively Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: About an hour later, tell us what happens.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An hour later, Tralja appeared, who already knew me since he had confiscated my car and robbed my house, and he told me, "What are you doing here?"

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did he do after that?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He brutally beat me all over my body. He threw me against metal cupboards where the archives of the police station were kept at that time. He really didn't care how and in what way he beat me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did he beat anyone else in addition to you?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Who, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that occasion, he beat Esad Mesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when he beat you, did he use his hands or did he use a weapon of any kind?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He beat me with whatever he could get his hands on, with his weapons, his feet, his hands, mostly in the region of the genitals and the region of my head. These were the most sensitive places.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And how long did that beating last?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly, but it lasted for as long as the first beating did, probably for about 15 or 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's continue on to about 1.00 a.m., in the early morning hours. Are you familiar with persons or soldiers named Laki and Nesa?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did they visit you later that day or into the early morning hours?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As you said yourself, it was about 1.00 in the morning. They came to get me and they told me to come out from that room. Of course, that's what I did, and I followed them. They took me upstairs to the first floor of the police building, to one of the offices, where they told me to sit down. And then they started to beat me brutally, to ask for money, ask for gold, which they had already confiscated from me. And they were telling me, "You want to make a Muslim state in the heart of Europe. You will never get a state like that."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did they use any weapons during this beating?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Tell the Tribunal what they did and what they used.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They mostly -- they were mostly pistols, automatic rifles, and it was an everyday occurrence to place those weapons pointed at our heads or in -- into our mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did they use any knives?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Tell the Court about that, please.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will tell you in which way they used it. They cut my ears. They cut my neck. They used a screwdriver, a screwdriver for unscrewing screws.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what did they do with that screwdriver?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They told me to -- he told me to place my hands, my palm down, on the table, and then he placed the screwdriver on the upper part of my hand, my fist, and he literally said, "Give me the money. Tell me where the money is or I will go right through your hand," and he did. He went right through my hand with the screwdriver. And I also would like to say, to go back to that knife, because Laki didn't have two fingers on one hand, he took a pencil and he drew the amount that his fingers were cut off, he drew that same amount on my hand, and he wanted to cut my fingers in the same way that his fingers were cut.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You said he stabbed you in the hand with a screwdriver?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did that cause any scarring?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Does that scar exist to this day?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could the witness come and show the judges and then Defence counsel the scar on his hand?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I was wondering whether he can use the ELMO and then the technicians maybe can --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I don't know if it will pick it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: If it won't, then he can come around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Maybe the witness can just walk around, because we can't --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dagovic, could you start off, show the Judges where the scar is and then to each of the Defence counsel, each of the Defence attorneys? Start off with the Judges, please. If you could approach each of the Judges first?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may the record reflect that the defendant has a small scar on his hand? Looks like the type of screwdriver we'd call a Phillips screwdriver in the United States, which is that cross type of screw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: On the right hand?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Is it the right or the left?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's on the right hand, and it was just a normal screwdriver. It wasn't a star screwdriver, but just a regular one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, because we were shown the right hand. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: The scar is on the back of the right hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Through the back.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir -- do you know a man by the name of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I agree that it can be stated that the witness has a scar on his hand, but we cannot state at this stage that that is the cause of the scar. At this stage, it can only be ascertained that there is a scar on his hand. We cannot use the wording proposed by the Prosecutor. Only the Court can rule whether this was the cause of the scar on his hand. And the witness's statement and other things have to be taken duly into account. So please, could the wording be different? Can it be stated that the witness has a scar on his right hand? I agree to that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I say something, please, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness say what he wants to say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since I'm in a country with a very good health system, I have gone through various examinations and check-ups. I can give you all these papers referring to my scar, and the gentleman can have a look at that. I have all of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't mind that. I'm just talking about this wording that we heard, and of course evidence should be provided and its probative value should be established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just stating that the record -- what the record reflected. There is a scar on the back of his hand, and that the -- and we've already heard testimony from the witness - the record speaks for itself - of where that scar comes from, from the stabbing with the screwdriver.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The record will reflect that the Court has noticed a scar on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Right hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: -- right hand of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, are you familiar with a man by the name of Josip Orsolic?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And how do you know Josip Orsolic?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Josip Orsolic -- excuse me. I know him from town. He was a neighbour of mine as well. He is a man of Catholic faith, a Croat, that is. He was an educated man and he was a man who held high positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did he do for work?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a while he was chief of police. Then he was general manager of a firm and then he opened a company of his own.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: During those early morning hours when you were beaten by Laki and Nesa, did you see Josip Orsolic?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Tell the Court what you saw.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They brought him to the same room where I was. They beat him very brutally. The same knife that they used for cutting my throat, my ears and my fingers, they used for cutting him too, and these cuts on his body were over one centimetre deep.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did they do with him?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't hear your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did they do with him after they beat him?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They told him that they would take him to his home now so that he could give them his money. So they took him away then, and we left together, and they left me in the room where they kept me before they took me upstairs. And then they took him out, probably to his house, because I heard the sound of a car.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see Josip Orsolic after that evening?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you hear whatever happened to Mr. Orsolic?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that he had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Have you ever seen him since that evening?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's return to the beating. The blows that you took, how much force was involved in those blows during that beating?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. The blows were administered with all their strength, as we would put it, and it's not only that they were strong. How should I put this? They hit the right spots, most sensitive parts of the body: the genitals, the face, the head. And what hurt me very much was behind the neck, and I still suffer from the consequences of that until the present day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you ever hit in the face?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How were you hit in the face?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They hit me with boots. They hit me in the jaw area. My jaw is displaced on account of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: During this beating, did they say anything?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were cursing our mothers, our Muslim, Croat mothers. They said vulgar words. They said that they would kill all of us. They were saying the worst things.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did they say anything about executing the educated people? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's just what I wanted to say. They said that they would kill all the smart Muslims and Croats so that only the stupid Muslims and Croats would be left behind, but they forgot that those stupid ones were smarter than them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How long did this beating last?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It lasted for a long time, perhaps an hour or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let us continue on in the month of May, about a week later, on May 13th. Were you still at the police station through the month of May?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you recall a visit by the Swiss or Red Cross or someone about a week after this beating?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Tell the Court about that, please.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I noticed that something was going on at the police building, or rather, that they were singling people out, separating them, the very beaten up ones and the old ones on one side and the other ones on the other. I was lucky enough to get to that room in a condition that was a bit better but that was not that good, and they established that. They Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. also registered me in their books, if I can call them that, and I was registered as being detained. As for these other people who were separated from us, they were hidden. And they gave us blankets so that they would show the International Red Cross that we are in a good position, that we have everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did they ask you any questions - meaning the Red Cross - ask you any questions concerning the conditions there?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Since we were afraid, we actually didn't know who they were, we sort of -- we didn't dare tell them. But they were more interested in the bloodstains on the walls and on the ceiling and on the floor. They asked us what that was. Of course, we didn't dare say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did they ask you about food, about bedding, any other questions?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Please tell us what they asked you and how you responded.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They asked us how we were doing there, whether we had any food, whether we were allowed to bathe, go to the toilet. Of course we said that everything was okay, although it wasn't. We had a little --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You had a little -- ? What was that? You had a little -- ? I'm sorry. The interpreter --

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that we had a little bucket, and we used that as a toilet, because we were not allowed to go to the toilet. We could not bathe, we could not shave, we didn't have anything, but we said to them that everything was okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Obviously, when you said everything was okay, that wasn't true. Why did you have to say something to them that wasn't true?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because we were afraid whether they were actually these people. I don't know. The chief of the police then could send some other people to see what we thought. I don't know. We were afraid, because we were exposed to torture and beatings every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you threatened prior to this visit? Were any threats made or ...

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in principle, they said that we should say that everything was all right, but -- it is obvious from the blankets that they gave us that we were supposed to say that everything was all right. They forced us to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you indicated some of the prisoners were not interviewed on that date.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They talked to the prisoners, but we did not dare say what the actual situation was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No. You said some of the certain prisoners were not interviewed; they were sent to another room.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what was their condition, their physical condition?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were in very bad shape. There were elderly people among them, too. That was probably the reason why they put them away.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when you say they were in bad shape, what had happened to them to get them into this bad shape?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had been brutally beaten, all broken up, literally. They could not stand on their own feet. Their faces were distorted beyond recognition from the blows that they had received.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: May we go into closed session for approximately five minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, we will go into closed session -- private session, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Private session, sorry, private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dagovic, let us continue into the month of June. Let us go to June 7th, to the morning of June 7th. Can you tell us what happened, as best you can recall?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime around 9.00 in the morning of the 7th of June, the so-called specials came, soldiers from Serbia, and they selected me and Dzemal Muric, nicknamed Dzemak, to come along with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what happened?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then we got out of the police station, then we got into their red BMW -- or was it their car, I doubt it. It must have been one of the plundered cars. And then we went in the direction of my house, or rather in the direction of Dr. Anto Majic's house, because he lived near me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, did you arrive at a location?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And at this doctor's home?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we got to Dr. Anto Majic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you know this Dr. Anto Majic?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And who did he live with?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He lived with his wife Zlata, his son Alan, and his daughter Anela.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And do you know what occupation his wife Zlata had?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She did work. She was either a doctor or a nurse. She also worked at the health centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were they home when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Where were they, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, Mrs. Majic, with her children, had already left Samac before that, or rather before the attack on Samac. And Mr. Anto Majic, at the beginning of the war, was in Samac. I saw him. And since then -- I mean after that, I never saw him again. But I hear that he is somewhere in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were they Croatians by nationality?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were Bosnian Croats, Catholics.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And could you describe the house? Was it a nice house? Was it -- as best you can to the Court.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My estimate was that this was one of the nicer houses in Samac. Not only that, it was really luxuriously appointed. That is to say, the right kind of house, as we would put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did you and Dzemal Muric do at that house?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the orders issued by these soldiers, or rather these specials, among who was a soldier from Samac, a member of the 4th Detachment, we had to throw all the things out of Dr. Majic's house on to the terrace of the house. When I say things, I'm referring to books, glassware, china. Everything that was in the cupboards and closets, we had to throw that out. And they left the piano so that they could play with it, so that they would have fun with it, so that they would have more fun, generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was there any search done of that house?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They probably searched that house, but while these things were being carried out, we found a certain amount of money.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How much money did you find?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We found a thousand Deutschmarks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What happened to that thousand Deutschmarks?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since they were sitting on sofas like sheriffs while we were working, at one moment, I dropped on the floor an ink pad for stamps, and inside was -- were a thousand Deutschmarks. Of course, they noticed that, and I handed these thousand Deutschmarks over to them. They were screaming, because they were so happy, like madmen, because perhaps they had not seen a thousand Deutschmarks before. So they split it up. It wasn't a single thousand Deutschemark bill. It was several bills. So they shared this among themselves; they split it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was there any itemisation made of the property, any receipts left for the money, any sort of documentation of that property that was in that house?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: While we are on the subject, sir, were you ever forced to loot homes as part of your forced labour?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was this prior to arrest?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was arrested, or rather when we were being taken from the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, how many homes were you forced to loot or plunder?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my estimate is that it was tens of houses. I remember some of the houses in particular because I knew these people well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were these homes -- or actually, of what nationality were these homes that were looted? The people who owned them or lived there, of what nationality were they?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The owners were Bosniak Muslims and Croat Catholics.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever loot any homes owned by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. We were just filling them with plundered goods.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When you looted these homes, what type of objects did you steal?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly it was technical equipment, precious jewellery, sometimes furniture, foodstuffs, money, fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When you say "technical equipment," do you mean like electrical-type appliances, or what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I am referring to music, like hi-fi sets, cameras, and refrigerators, various ovens, washing machines and other appliances.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, would you like to take a break here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. It's 11.00, and we'll continue at 11.30 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Examination-in-chief by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dagovic, before we went into our recess, you were discussing how you were forced to loot or steal from the homes of Croatians and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Aziz Hacimovic?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Who was that person? Tell the Court.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Aziz Hacimovic, called Ciger, worked at the petrol station.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Is it a man or a woman?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a man.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us what happened in relation to his home?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At one time a police officer called Pero Stefanovic, I think his last name is, and he told us that we have to go with them. He came with two other police officers. Myself, Antica Bauman, and Sabah Seric went with them. We drove towards the part of the town that is called Donja Mahala, to the house of Mr. Aziz Hacimovic and his mother. We went into the house and we were ordered to take out those things that they happened to like, and those things were mostly foods, technical equipment, and money and gold. Since Mr. Hacimovic worked at the gas station, they also found petrol, which he had probably brought to his house to have a supply of his own, because before the war there was a shortage of petrol, and we also had to take that. And I know that Aziz's old mother, who was a woman of perhaps 60 or -- between 60 and 70 years of age, she begged me and cried, asking me to leave at least some of the food. On that occasion I managed to leave one litre of oil and a little bit of flour for her, and everything else we took away.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So when you arrived at that home to loot it, his mother was home, his mother was in the house?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did she ask them not to take anything, or just you?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She begged them, but since she had the opportunity, as she knew me, because she is part of an old family in Samac, so she knew my family, she knew me, so she asked me to leave something for her. And you can imagine how I felt when she did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, do you know a man by the name of Rade Borovo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, when a witness, because of the terms of expression in everyday language, says, "You can imagine how I felt," can you please let him explain how he felt?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you explain how you felt at that time, sir, when you -- when the woman was crying and pleading with you?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I felt terrible, in the sense that, in other words, at that time, I was the same as they were, a looter, a criminal, even though I wasn't like that. I was forced to do that. So I had to do what they told me to do. I felt very bad. It seemed to me as if I didn't have any strength. I felt like I would fall. That's how I felt.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You indicated the police took you to loot that home. Were those local police officers from Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, amongst them was this person called Pero.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch his last name.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But he was an active police officer before the war so they were police officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The interpreter said they didn't catch the last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's what I was going to ask, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you know the last name of this Pero, this police officer named Pero?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First I said Pero Stefanovic, but he's actually Pero Krstanovic and he was from Novo Selo. It's a village near Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When you went to these numbers of homes to loot, what did you do with the items after you took them out of homes?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We loaded them into a truck. The gold, they took in the front with them, where the driver was, and I don't know what they did with that gold and the money. But I know that we took the items and the food. Some of them we took to the police station, to the SUP, and the rest they took somewhere else. I don't know where, because they dropped us off on the way back at the police station or the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When you say "they," "they" took or these people that appear to be supervising this, who is "they"? Were these police? Were they soldiers? Who is "they"?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that occasion, they were police officers, as I have already said. So when I say "they," I mean them, the police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What about on the other occasions?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will also tell you about another occasion. At one time as you already mentioned, Rade Borovo -- Rade was his first name, and Borovo was his nickname, that's what they called him. He took us to the house of Muhamed Kuburic in the same part of town, in Donja Mahala. Mr. Kuburic had a very nice house. It was nicely decorated. He also had a shop. And on orders of Rade Borovo, we were forced to load coal and articles of food from that shop of his. And from that shop, we took the items to the garage of Rade Borovo. The garage was part of the building complex known as 62, sezdesetdvojka. That is what we called the buildings. And Mr. Rade was a member of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What type of shop did the victim of this looting or plunder have?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was like a general store. All kinds of food articles were being sold there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You indicated that you did a looting with a member of the 4th Detachment, some police officers. Were any of these lootings involving the soldiers, whether they are the local soldiers or the Serbian specials?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This time, there was Rade Borovo. He was a member of the 4th Detachment, but we also went on several occasions with members of the Special Forces, with the soldiers from the Republic of Serbia, and also we went frequently with the soldiers of the so-called 4th Detachment. At one time, I went to Odzak. That time we were taken there by the members of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what did you do in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Odzak fell, when it fell into the hands of the paramilitaries of Republika Srpska, we went there to empty the houses, as they popularly called it. Since the Serbian soldiers were afraid of bombs, which were sometimes placed inside the door or at the entrance to the houses, we were the first to enter the house. They probably thought if we get killed, it's not too much of a shame. So that's -- on those occasions, we mostly carried out coal, furniture, other items, the equipment and the radiators for central heating, the furnaces, we even stripped the parquet flooring from the houses and took that away.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How many of these houses in Odzak were you forced to loot or plunder?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tens of houses. I don't know the number but it was a lot of houses. And this is what it would more or less look like. When the truck would go, there would be two or three of us forced to do the forced labour. The truck would stop from one house to the next. In one street there could be 50 houses, 20, 10, depending on the street, and then we would enter into each of the houses and carry out the things that they liked.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether these houses were populated by or had been owned by people of what nationality?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the homes were abandoned, we even found the remains of an uneaten lunch at the kitchen table. Then we could -- we are talking about homes of Muslims and the homes of Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did you do with this property after you loaded it -- I assume you loaded it on a truck, this property from Odzak, that came from the homes in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, whether the 4th Detachment or the police issued certificates to its soldiers, I don't know, but I know that certificates were issued permitting soldiers or police officers to take coal to their own houses, the coal plundered from those Muslim and Croat houses. So that means that we would take those items to the houses of the police officers and the soldiers. We would have to unload those goods and also take the coal to the cellar or wherever the proper place was for that coal to be kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, were you involved in the looting of any of the property owned by Muhamed or Hasan Bicic?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court about that, please.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since they knew I worked at the pizzeria, at Hasan Bicic's pizzeria, they assumed that I knew everything that he had, and I did know everything that he had, because I told you yesterday that we were like brothers. They took me to his house, where there was a large storage room where he kept goods: food articles, beverages, all the things that were necessary for the operation of a restaurant. I had to load these goods, on several occasions, had to load them into trucks and take them away. Also, in the yard of his house there was a garage which was locked. I had to break down the door, and that's where we kept the petrol. As I said before, since there had been a petrol shortage and it was difficult to get petrol, we had a small supply of petrol there so that we could drive the cars. This was probably not enough for them, so they would also take me to the pizzeria, and at the pizzeria I also had to load the items that I had previously, before I had been arrested and taken to the camp, had, with the help of my brother, and with the help of Enes Mahic, another worker at the pizzeria, which I had taken down into the cellar, with the intention of saving some of the things so that they would not be plundered and robbed. So those things I had to load into the truck once again so that they could take those things away, and I don't know where they took them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when you said "they," who were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am thinking about police officers and sometimes soldiers of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How did you feel about looting your close friend's property?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I felt as if I were robbing my own property, and by that I mean to say that this is where, at that pizzeria -- the pizzeria was a place where I earned my daily bread, and I could see that this tower of my source of income was being toppled in all this looting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, let us return to the doctor's home on June 7th.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And at this time, Your Honour, can we return to closed session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Private session, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You were brought back to the police station; correct?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: As of this date, you had now been held in the police station for one month, a little over one month, sir?
