utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did anyone tell you why you were being held?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, I was taken to an informative talk, and it lasted a few months. There was no particular reason other than the fact that I was a Bosniak, a Muslim. I don't believe that I had done anything to anybody. I was young. I was 22 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you a member of the military at that time?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you're back at the station. What were you doing after you got back to the station?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I returned to the station and after we came back, we immediately left for another job, and this other job was to clean weapons. I cleaned weapons, and at one point, Slobodan Miljkovic, called "Lugar," appeared. He looked like a madman, and by that I mean that he was enraged, his eyes were bloodshot and he was drunk. He started to abuse people and to beat them. One of those beaten and abused people was Ridvan Dzakic, called Ridvo. He's a cousin of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did he do to Mr. Dzakic?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He beat him. He beat him with everything, including his silencer on his sniper rifle, which I estimate was about 40 centimetres in length. He used all objects that he found to beat him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: After he beat Mr. Dzakic, what did he do?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then he started to beat me. He literally said, "You Brkica, you with the beard, come here." And I went up to him and he asked me what did I do. I meant -- I thought that with that question he meant what I was doing at that moment, at the time that I was at the police station, and I said I was cleaning weapons. And he started to beat me like an animal. He beat me with all kinds of things, amongst other things a suspension device from the car which he found on the floor. He beat me with metal bars. He also beat me with a tool, a spanner. It was a very difficult -- a very heavy and large spanner. And he beat me in the area of the head, also all over my body, on my genitals. This wasn't enough for him. Each time, he would pick me up off the floor, pretty high, and then throw me back down on the ground. This even wasn't enough for him. Then he would do the same thing again. He would lift me up into the air and then throw me down over his knee. Maybe he wanted to break my back. I don't know. [redacted].

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: [redacted], let me ask you a couple of questions. When you say he hit you with a suspension device, is that commonly known as a shock absorber?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did he do anything to your teeth?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He took out my teeth.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How did he take out your teeth?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since we were repairing cars there, that is to say that there were tools there as well. He pulled my teeth out with pliers. He broke my teeth with the barrel of an automatic rifle, or rather with the sight of an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How many teeth were pulled from your mouth?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How long did this beating last?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to my estimate, could have been around half an hour or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: [redacted]?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did say that, but I would like to go back to myself again. When I was lying on the ground then, he took a pistol out, TT 762. He cocked it, he put it against my forehead with the intention of killing me. At that moment, his colleague, a soldier, appeared, another special like he was, nicknamed Debeli. And then this man addressed Slobodan Miljkovic, called Lugar, and said, "It's all right. Don't kill him." And he walked up to me, and he said that I should go to the station. [redacted]

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [redacted]. And then he started beating me ferociously, like an animal, and that's when he put the pistol against my forehead with the intention of killing me, probably, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: [redacted]?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: 23. [redacted] So Lugar started taking it out on him. He started beating him. He called him a Ustasha Croat motherfucker. He beat him with all sorts of things and in all parts of the body.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: After Debeli stops him from shooting you, what does Lugar do with the gun?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lugar, as I said, [redacted] [redacted], he took out that same pistol and put it on his head, and he fired. Only a click sound was heard. He was furious. I realised that his pupils had opened and that his eyes were really big, like the eyes of a savage. He again cocked the pistol, and the bullet fell on to the ground. He took it, and it was obvious that the bullet had not fired. Again he cocked his pistol, and he fired into the air. And this was -- this confirmed that the gun was all right but that there was something wrong with the bullet. [redacted], "You're really lucky today. I'm not going to kill you today." And then he left.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When he fired into the ceiling, did the gun actually fire, discharge at that time?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: On the previous time you said he cocked it and the bullet fell out or slipped out, did it fall out of the front of the gun, the barrel, or from the chamber? Or was it one where you cocked it and it fell out of the chamber? Please explain what you mean.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A bullet cannot fall out of a barrel. That would have meant that it was fired. He opened the pistol backwards, he cocked his pistol again after that, and then the bullet fell out of the barrel, and then this -- and then it was obvious that the hammer had hit the capsule of the bullet and that the bullet had not fired. [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: At this point, when he leaves, when Lugar leaves, what is your condition [redacted]?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [redacted]I - I don't know how - barely walked, escorted by a guard to the cell where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What happened once you got back to the cell?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since there were around 49 persons in my cell, I'm trying to say that we did not have enough room to sit. We had to stand on one foot only, several of us, and then we'd take turns. The prisoners, the others in this room, they made room for me so that I could be put on the ground. We didn't have any beds, of course, but they let me lie down, and they stood this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What was your physical condition at that time as you were lying on the ground?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in a very bad physical condition. I was bleeding from the nose, ears and mouth. Every part of my body was in pain, as if somebody had taken the flesh off my bones. When these blows, as I would put it, had cooled off, then it hurt so badly that I was swearing at the guards, trying to provoke them so that they would kill me. However, one of the specials said to me, "We are not going to kill you. We are going to let you suffer."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Why did you want them to kill you?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I had these terrible pains. I could not breathe. I was bleeding from the mouth. I felt terrible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How long did you remain lying on that floor? Tell the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remained lying until the next day, that is to say the 8th of June, 1992, and I was moaning so badly from the pain that the policeman on duty called Dimitrij called an ambulance, or rather a doctor, and he came. The doctor who came -- actually, I can't remember his name, his first name, but his last name was Stevic, he was the son of Stevo Stevic, who was a doctor in Bosanski Samac before the war. He examined me, and I know that he looked at me, and he said that I had to go to hospital. And then he left. After perhaps about an hour, an ambulance came and they carried a stretcher into the building where I was, or rather the cell where I was, they put me on this stretcher and they carried me out, accompanied by inmates, or rather the inmates carried me out - it was probably too hard for them - and they drove me to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Which hospital did you go to, and where was that hospital located?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was one single hospital in Samac. I think the street used to be called the street of Edvard Kardelj. It was on the outskirts of Samac, on the road to the villages of Crkvina and Pisarevo, on the right-hand side of that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When you got to the hospital, did anyone treat you?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Tell the Court what happened at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I got to the hospital - I must say this once again - I was received cordially and nicely by the doctor of Serb ethnicity called Mirko Sisic. I keep saying this. I will never forget the way this man received me. I know that he said, furious, "What are they doing to our people?" I was taken to a room where there were two other patients who were ethnic Serbs, and I must say that, with the assistance of Dr. Mirko Sisic, I had all the medicine required and everything I needed. What Dr. Sisic underlined to me, or rather, what he said to me, was that I should never say to anyone that I was a prisoner but that I should say that I had been in a traffic accident, and that's what I did, because in the hospital, in the hospital -- actually, soldiers were coming to that hospital, Serbs soldiers, so I had to be careful.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did they do to you in the hospital to diagnose what your problems were? Did they -- what did they do when you got there? What type of tests did they run, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Sisic ordered an x-ray to be made straight away of the lungs and the bones. It was established that my ribs were broken. It was established that my pelvic bone was broken, and therefore I could not walk. That's why I was in a wheelchair.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you have any problems with your lungs?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Tell the Court.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since my lungs were bleeding, there was some kind of an infection, or rather, pneumonia. In addition to all of that, I had to be treated for pneumonia. And this also has to do with sleeping on the cold floor, on the concrete floor in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you have any lung injury which caused the bleeding?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Probably, or rather, as he had put it to me, a rib was stuck in the lung, so that is to say that this broken rib had punctured the lung.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you have a pelvis bone, broken ribs, a punctured lung. What about the rest of your body, the rest of your back? Any other injuries to your back, to your hands, to your feet, to your legs? Any other injuries, sir?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I just wanted to say that. The finger on my right hand was broken.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you able to walk?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did you use to get around in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said previously, in a wheelchair.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How long were you in that hospital?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in hospital from the 8th of June until the 8th of July, that is to say, one month.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How were you treated for the pneumonia? Tell the Court.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, in view of the privileges accorded to me by Mr. Sisic, I had everything. I got IV twice a day, probably some kind of medicine and something to make me stronger, that was administered in the vein; and also I got penicillin in the morning and in the evening, 60 milligrams; and also I often got painkiller shots. And what was another privilege: There was a Muslim woman who was working there. She was my neighbour. She was a nurse. So in addition to Dr. Sisic, who really did his best to have me cured, she gave me extra painkiller shots.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you familiar with a man by the name of Hasan Hadzialijagic?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: While you were in the hospital, did you see Hasan Hadzialijagic?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How old was that gentleman, approximately?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That gentleman was perhaps over 50 at the time. I knew that man well, because he was a native of Samac, like myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Why did you see him at the hospital? Tell the Court.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in very bad shape, like myself. He told me that he had been beaten by the Serb soldiers, that he was brought to hospital. What I managed to see on him was that he had trouble breathing, that he had sustained bodily injuries, that he was black and blue in the body, as we would put it. And there is something that remains imprinted in my memory, and I still see this until the present day. He had these big scars on his stomach where they had extinguished cigarettes. I know that he could not go to the toilet. I don't know why he couldn't. Perhaps due to the blows he had sustained. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Also during that month that you were in the hospital, did you ever see a man by the name of -- or nicknamed Suma?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How old was Suma?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Suma was in his 40s, approximately. I knew that man well because he lived in my street, where my maternal grandmother lived too, my mother's mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And was Suma incarcerated with you?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Suma was incarcerated at the Territorial Defence headquarters of the former Yugoslav People's Army, that is to say, in the other camp across the street from the SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What about Hasan Hadzialijagic, whom you just mentioned? Was he incarcerated with you?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, Hasan was brought from home. He was beaten up in the street. And after that he was probably locked up. I didn't see him after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's return to Suma. You saw Suma at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Suma was in the same room where I was, opposite my bed. That's where he was lying.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In what condition was Suma, if you can best describe it?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. As we would put it, he was a bag of bones. I don't know if he weighed 40 kilos, perhaps 50. He was very skinny. It is true that he was thin before, but at that time he was really skinny. He could not walk. He was throwing up. He couldn't eat. He was in very, very, very bad shape.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you what had happened to him to cause him to be in this very bad shape?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did he say?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said to me that he had been beaten at the Territorial Defence building and that the specials and the soldiers beat him; among others, Slobodan Miljkovic, nicknamed Lugar, that he beat him, and when he beat him with his hands and weapons, and he kicked him with his feet. And even that wasn't enough. He jumped on his stomach. So Suma was lying on his back and this person was jumping on his stomach, with all his weight.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What happened to Suma at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Suma soon died. He died in my arms, because he was suffering terrible pain. Every time he was in greater pain, I would come up to him, and that time I lifted his head a bit so that he would get a bit of air. Actually, I did not have any experience with dying persons. And he was struggling with his own soul, and he died in my arms. I called Dr. Sisic. He came and concluded that Suma had died, that he had passed away.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When did he die in relation to his telling you that Lugar had beaten him, Lugar and the other paramilitaries had beaten him?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after a few days maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Of what ethnic nationality was Suma and Hasan Hadzialijagic?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both of them were Bosniak Muslims by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You just mentioned Lugar. Do you know where Lugar came from?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Please tell us.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He came from Kragujevac, and he liked it when they called him Sumadinac, a man from Sumadija.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you or tell anyone what he did in Kragujevac?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard -- actually, I overheard some of the soldiers, as they were talking amongst themselves when I was cleaning the corridors or distributing food, I heard that Slobodan Miljkovic, nicknamed Lugar, was a boxer and that he was boxing for a club in Kragujevac, and I must admit that he looked like a boxer, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Why do you say he looked like a boxer? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was very well-developed, and he had a boxer's nose.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Meaning a flat nose or --

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you ever present when Lugar murdered anyone?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Tell the Court, please, what happened.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was taken to work at Hrvatska Tisina, at the stadium. I had to take the parts off an abandoned car, an old abandoned car there. At one moment, a truck came with people in the truck. I assumed that they were all ethnic Croats, because I did not know these people and since Tisina was a Croat village. Well, this is where Miljkovic took a man out of the truck, an elderly man, and he simply took out his rifle -- took out his pistol and killed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Where did he shoot him with this pistol? Where did he shoot the victim?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I managed to see, he shot him in the chest, or between the chest and the head. Was it the neck?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The man died?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see Lugar beating prisoners?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And can we have the time period when the killing happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You heard Her Honour's question. Can you tell us when this occurred? Was this prior to your arrest, after your arrest, if you can even tell us a month?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. This was after the arrest, but I can't remember the date. At any rate, it was after I was in hospital. I know that for sure, because after I was in hospital, I was assigned to the garage. I was in the working group that repaired cars. I went to take parts off cars. This was after the month of July, that is. Perhaps it was the month of August. I really can't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Because I was wondering about the time period, because I was wondering whether the witness -- after he was released from hospital, did he go back to the detention?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We were going to get back to that after Lugar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let me just jump ahead on a few questions. We will step away from Lugar for a moment. You left the hospital on what date?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hospital? Around the 7th of July, a policeman named Dragan Stefanovic from the village of Crkvina came to me and he asked me, or rather said to me that the Red Cross was asking whether I wanted to go for an exchange. And I said yes. And he said that he would pick me up. And then on the next day, the 8th of June [sic], he came back to collect me and took me back to hospital.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness first said the 7th of July and then the 8th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The next day, he took you -- you said he took you back to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Weiner, can you -- we are told by the interpreter that the witness first said the 7th of July and then the 8th of June. Can you clarify that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm trying to. I'm confused. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The police officer visited you on July 7th?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the 7th of July. Perhaps I made a mistake, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What happens to you after you speak to the police officer?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, he asked me whether I wanted to go to be exchanged. He said to me that this was a question that was put by the Red Cross. And I said yes. And he left, and he said that he'd come and get me. He said that he would come back on the next day, that is to say the 8th of July. He drove me away in a car. I know whose car it was. It was a civilian car. And he drove me back to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when you say he drove you back to the camp, where did he take you on July 8th?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, how long did you remain in the police station?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until I was exchanged on November 5th, 1992, which means that I was deceived.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: On July 7th, you mean? When you say you were deceived, did you mean on July 7th, when he asked you if you wanted to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. They told me I was going to be exchanged. And I said yes. And under those circumstances, I left the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But not for the exchange, would you have left the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because I wasn't really fit at that point to leave the hospital. And if you permit me to say, Dr. Sisic -- after that police officer left, Dr. Sisic told me that I had made a mistake and that I wasn't fit enough, well enough, to leave the hospital and that I will probably not be exchanged. Perhaps he spoke on the basis of his experience. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Between July 8th and when you were exchanged on November 5th, as best as you can determine, when did the murder of the elderly man occur?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like I say, perhaps it was in mid-July or in August. I know it was very hot later. I remember that very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let us return to Lugar, Mr. Miljkovic. Did you ever see Lugar beating any prisoners at the police station?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Tell the Court what you saw Lugar doing at the police station.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He used to beat the prisoners. It seems to me that he was the one who beat the prisoners the most. Do I need to say the names of those people?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You can mention some of them that he beat.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would start with a father, Father Jozo Puskaric, who was a parish priest in Hrvatska Tisina. He beat him fiercely. He beat him like an animal. He told him, "God sent you to teach people the faith and to calm people down, and instead, you are inciting them against the Serbs," which was not true. I know that that man -- both of his eyes and ears were closed from the beating. He was swollen from the beating. He was blue all over. He had lost a lot of weight, but he was psychologically very strong. I don't know if it was of some help to him that he was a man of religion. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: This priest that Lugar beat, did he get along with the other prisoners, such as the Muslim prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That man was an inspiration to us. I viewed him -- since he was older than me, I looked upon him as if he were my father. He was an honest man. And he said -- when we managed to bring in food with the help of good guards, we would give this food to him so that he could distribute it amongst us nicely so that each one of us would receive something, because we were hungry most of the time, and perhaps we would even dare to take a greater, a larger share, but he was the one who would give everybody the portion so that everybody would receive equal parts. Some of the prisoners mentioned suicide. However, he said that this is something that should not be considered, that there will come a time when these stories will need to be told, and now I say thank God that moment is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In addition to the priest, who else did Lugar beat at the police station?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He beat a lot of people, but what sticks in my mind is a professor, a teacher of English. His name was Mirko. I don't know his surname. I know that he was from Croatia, I think from Slavonski Brod. He used to tell him that he was a Ustasha spy, and he beat him a lot, so that this man's head was twice the size, because it was swollen so much from the beating. I know that he made him to translate the rules of the -- the code of conduct of the former Yugoslav army in order to be sure that he was an English teacher, even though everybody knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What was his age, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was between 40 and 50 years old, but I'm not really sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What did Lugar beat you and all these other prisoners with?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said before, he didn't care how he beat us, where he beat us, what he beat us with. He used everything. But not only his, but the favourite of others also was when they tied us to a chair so that they would push our feet through towards the back of the chair, and that's how they would tie us up, and then they would beat us on the soles of our feet and also on the backs of our hands so that our soles and the backs of our hands were very swollen, and it was very painful. But compared to the others, Lugar was very destructive, and I mean that in the sense that, as I've already said, he was a boxer, so he would mostly strike us on our head. He would also beat us on the other parts of the body. And when he hit us, the -- we would fall down. He would use metal bars, guns, the baseball bats, anything that was near, near him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: With the Court's permission, could he demonstrate how they were tied in the chairs and had to sit so they could beat their hands and feet?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dagovic, could you demonstrate as best you could with that chair?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It looked something like this. This chair is a little wider. The other chairs were narrower. So we would have to sit like this, place our feet towards the back. We would be tied up here and also our legs would be tied in the back. And then they would beat us on the soles of our feet. Of course, we would have to take our shoes off. Of course, this chair is broader and it's more luxurious than the chairs they used. So this is how they would tie us up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may the record reflect that the witness is sitting with his feet under him, under his buttocks, facing the rear, facing behind him, which would give someone the opportunity to strike the soles of the feet from behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you also struck on your hands, too? Did you have to --

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you have to keep your hands out? Were your hands tied? Explain what you had to do with your hands.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our hands were tied, yes, depending on the kind of chair, whether it had arm rests or not. If it did have an arm rest, this is how they would be tied. If not, this is how they would be tied, with our palms on the inside so they could beat us on the backs of our hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness just demonstrated that his hands would be tied, the palms somehow behind, and his palms would be facing outward so his hands could be beaten along the backs of his hands. The palms would be inward so he could be beaten on the backs of his hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, as demonstrated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Where did these beatings occur at the police station?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the police station, before the war, had a part that was a prison, a part of it was a prison, the rest of us were detained in offices, so we would be beaten in these offices. We would be beaten in the corridors, in the yard, as I say, in the yard that was behind the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How many people did Lugar take out at any one time to beat?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my estimate, I think that there was not a single prisoner that Lugar did not beat.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were people beaten one at a time or in groups?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would beat people in groups and he would beat them one by one. He would simply enter the room and he would ask you your name, and you would say your name and then he would beat you; and then he would go to the next person, ask them their name, and then they would beat them. Mainly he disliked the names that he was told because they were not Serbian names. If I am permitted to add, I know that there was a person who was detained. He was a German citizen. He was a driver. He beat him a lot; not only he, but all the others beat this person a lot. They told him he was a homosexual. The man told me that they had taken 4.000 German marks from him, that they had taken his truck, that they had taken his passport. With all that beating, when the police officers, when the soldiers would come, we had to sing Chetnik songs. I never used to sing them before. I didn't know them. But there I was forced to learn them. He, however, was given five minutes' time to learn a Chetnik song, which of course is impossible, because the man didn't speak our language. They really beat him a lot. He had nothing to do with anything. I know that at one time they said, "We were killed -- Hitler killed us in World War II," and now they were retaliating for this, even though this man had nothing to do with Republika Srpska, with Yugoslavia, with anything. So there was no reason to do that to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How often did you have to sing Chetnik --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, my colleague. This is page 66, line 14. We heard that the witness said -- referring to Republika Srpska, he said, in his own native language, "so-called Republika Srpska." Could my learned friend clarify whether this witness said that or not, with regard to the Republika Srpska. Just as a matter of clarification in the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Would you like me to do that, or do you want to wait for cross-examination to have counsel do it, or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. Because I think it's a question of correcting the transcript, if he did say that. Maybe it wasn't just interpreted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, when you testified that this German that was a prisoner had nothing to do with the Republika Srpska, did you state "Republika Srpska" or "the so-called Republika Srpska"?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said "so-called Republika Srpska," because it was made by force at that time, and this is as clear as day. I can also say that at that time, the Serb formations were paramilitary formations, because in 1992 there was no Republika Srpska, if the gentleman didn't know this. And Bosnia was a recognised state.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the gentleman didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Sorry. I wish to thank the witness. Maybe I didn't know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. You're not supposed to do that, Mr. Pantelic. Please behave yourself, okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, how often did you have to sing Chetnik or Serbian patriotic songs?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that a single day passed that we didn't sing them, several times a day perhaps. Mostly when the Special Forces came, when the soldiers came, then we had to sing them out loud so that everybody could hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How long did you have to sing them? How long were these singing sessions?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know what? Sometimes they would come in and just say, "Song," and we knew what to do, and then we would not stop until they said, "Stop." So when one song would finish, we would start again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What was the longest period, if you can recall, that you had to sing these songs?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know precisely, but we would sing those songs for hours; not every day for hours, but there were times when we did sing them for hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's talk about the police station where you were held. Prior to April 17th, 1992, had you ever gone to the police station?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And for what reason would you go to the police station?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, when I was supposed to pick up my firearms licence for firearms that I had legally, or to pick up my driver's licence, or pick up my personal ID card or extend it. At one time I was on the first floor of the police station when I was taking my driver's test, the theoretical part of the driving exam.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In the summer of 1992, was the police station used for that same purpose?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no. It was purely a camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when you say "a camp," do you mean a prison camp or a Detention Centre, or what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A prison camp, yes. Detention would mean something that was of short duration, and prison camp is something that is for a longer period of time. We were there, we were kept there, for months.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were only men kept in that prison camp known as the police station?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Who else was kept there?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They kept women on certain occasions, and out of them two were detained there for a long time. The others were there briefly, for a day or two. I don't know where they would take them after that, but those two women were there for longer. I don't know exactly how long they were there, but I know that they were there for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court about the two women that were held at the police station.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew both of those women. One of them was in her 30s. Her name was Nihada Ademovic, and she worked at the department store as a saleswoman. And since she was from Gradacac, from a place which is close to Bosanski Samac, and her husband was from Samac, when the war started, she tried to go to Gradacac, because that's where her husband and children were. Since she was driving her car alone, she was by herself in the car, she told me that they took the German marks that she had, that they confiscated her car, and that they brought her to the camp. The other person, whom I also knew - I don't know her last name. I know her name is Behka - she worked with my mother at the textile company which is called Tekstilac. And at that time, if anything was funny to me, and at the same time it was funny and it was sad -- so this is what happened: They accused this woman of being a sniper. Some of the people know that woman, just as much as I know her, and they know that that woman didn't weigh more than 30 or 40 kilogrammes, 50 at the most, and they know that she couldn't even pick up a sniper, never mind fire from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Of what ethnic group were these women that were being held?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were Muslim. They were Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were either one of them in the military?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were either one of them wearing uniforms, military uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How would you characterise them?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean these women?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The woman who I described as being in her 30s, she was very pretty. She had brown hair. And as I said, before the war she always took care of herself. She always looked very nice. She was -- while she was in the camp, she wasn't able to do that, so she was unkempt. The other woman was in her 50s. She was very, very, and once again, very thin. She was blond. And as I said, she was so thin that she had trouble walking down the street even before the war. So really, she was very, very skinny.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were both of these women civilians?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see any other women or any elderly people being held at the police station?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Tell the Court.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I often had the honour to clean the rooms or the corridors -- I say I had the honour because perhaps a lot of the prisoners would like to have been able to do that in order just to walk around a little bit. So I used to clean one stairway that went all the way down to the cellar, to the basement. So I went down to the basement then and I heard some voices there, and I went a little bit further inside the basement and I saw that older men and women were detained there. They were wearing Croatian national costume, which is what the Croatian women from the surrounding villages would usually wear.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us -- could you please describe to the Court these Croatian national costumes, or the Croatian form of dress.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The women would mostly wear black clothes, black long skirts with a white lining. They would wear black tops with a white collar, or something like that, and they also had white head scarves, and one of them would perhaps have a black head scarf. And you could tell by their accent whether they were from Bazik or Grebnice. Their dialect, their accent, was different from ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were there any other prison camps that you're aware of in Bosanski Samac in addition to the police station?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Please tell the Court where those were.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A camp next to the camp in the police station was situated in the building where the TO was and the former JNA. The second -- or the third camp was at the secondary school, at the high school, and it was popularly called isolation. The fourth camp -- I have to make a correction here. Before I was arrested, there was a camp at the elementary school, which was closed down, and these people were then moved to the secondary school. There was another camp at a village called Zasevica. It was a Croat, Catholic village. That's where there was a camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You said that the secondary school was called "isolation." Why was it referred to as "isolation"?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you know who was held in Zasevica?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They kept women there, children, even babies, elderly people, the sick, old women, old men. They kept them all there. Mostly -- not mostly, but over 90 per cent of the people there were family members of the people who were detained in other places. And I think they wanted to round off the ethnic cleansing in the sense of exchanging entire families. And this is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When you returned to the police station, where were you kept?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean when I came back from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When you came back from the hospital, where were you kept?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I returned from the hospital, I was placed in garage 3. That garage was in the yard of the police station, behind the police station building, in the yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What was the yard behind the police station used for?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 1 was mostly used as a place where people were beaten up, also where people were put on the repair -- number 2 was where they repaired the cars. Number 3 was where the prisoners were held.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, would you like us to break here before we get into the yard a little bit more?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We can break off and continue our proceedings this afternoon at 1530 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m. 22 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, examination in chief is continuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Dagovic. Just before we broke for lunch, we were talking about the yard behind the police station with the garages, and you indicated that when you got back from the hospital, that you were placed in those -- one of those garages. How long did you stay in one of those garages? How long were you held there?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there until I was exchanged on November 5th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: During that period, from July 8th to November 5th, 1992, were you forced to do any type of labour while you were held in those garages?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Tell the Court what type of labour that you were forced to do.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, we had to -- and under forced labour, I'm also thinking of the looting and robbery, as I called it. We also had to clean, repair cars, wash cars of the police officers, the soldiers, all the worst jobs. We would cut wood, clean weapons, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: While you were doing these forced labour assignments, were you ever beaten?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Tell the Court, please, what happened.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each time while we were working, anybody that would walk -- who would walk by would hit us with something that they happened to be carrying in their hand, or if they had nothing, they would kick us or hit us with their hand. And we called it a banana, us inmates, and this just meant that you got hit just sort of as a kind of aside as somebody was passing by.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When you say "when someone was passing by," do you mean civilians, do you mean soldiers, do you mean police officers? Who were the people who would strike you during the forced labour?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were soldiers or the guards who were guarding us, who were there, who were watching over us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, were these guards or soldiers local ones or were those the ones from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to say it again, it was mostly people from the Special Forces, people from Serbia, but there were also many local Serbs or members of the 4th Detachment. It depended on where we were working. If we were in the town, for example, then there were soldiers there, locals, if I can call them that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And while you did this work, did you ever have to sing Chetnik songs? You indicated while you were being detained, you had to sing Chetnik songs. What about during the forced labour?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say that during the forced labour, they hardly ever made us sing the Chetnik songs. Perhaps occasionally, but it didn't happen as many times as it did when we were in the camp itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, prior to being imprisoned, and during your time of imprisonment, when you had to do forced labour, because you did it at both periods -- first, just answer this in a yes or no question. Did you ever see any of the defendants while you were doing or performing this forced labour?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let us start off with Blagoje Simic. Did you ever see Blagoje Simic while you were doing your forced labour?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Tell the Court where, and what the circumstances were.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once I was performing labour at the municipal building, and I can tell you the name of the person who took us there for forced labour. His name was Stevan. He worked at the municipality. And I saw Mr. Blagoje Simic entering the municipal building accompanied by some people, but I don't know who those people were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How was the defendant Blagoje Simic dressed?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was wearing a uniform, a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The men who were accompanying him, were they carrying any weapons?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How many times while you were performing forced labour did you see Blagoje Simic?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As often as I was there. So I was at the municipal building a couple of times, or somewhere in town, and I would see him passing by or entering the municipal building. But as I said, I saw him frequently at the municipal building. Because high-ranking officials often visited there, the premises had to be very clean, so this is where we were working, to make sure that everything was very clean.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Milan Simic, the defendant Milan Simic, did you ever see him while you were out on forced labour?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And where did you see Milan Simic?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time I saw Milan Simic in the yard, in my neighbour's yard, and this was before I was arrested. A young man from Sarajevo just happened to be there. He was visiting my neighbour, who was a Muslim, and my other neighbour was a Serb. His name was Teso, and Milan Simic was visiting him. On that occasion - and I knew Mr. Milan Simic very well - I asked if he could do something about this young man, and I meant if he could help this young man somehow leave town, because he had nothing to do with our town or the events in the town itself. And he told me that he could, and he issued a permit for this young man to leave town. The second time -- I mean, I saw him several times at the municipal building, as he was entering the building, and that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And how was he dressed when you saw Milan Simic?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see the defendant Miroslav Tadic while you were out doing forced labour?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And where did you see Miroslav Tadic?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him in different places around town, because we happened to be at different places, so I would see him as he was passing by.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And how was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wore a camouflage uniform. And something that was very noticeable to me, since I knew that gentleman from before, he had grown a long beard and he had longer hair and he was wearing round glasses, different ones that he's wearing now, and he resembled General Draza Mihajlovic from World War II. It seemed to be his image at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Simo Zaric, did you ever see the defendant Simo Zaric while you were doing your forced labour outside the station?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And tell the Court where you saw Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used to see Simo Zaric, besides seeing him in passing or around the town, I saw him at the silo once when we were working there. I saw him often at the police station, or the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When you were outside, did you ever see Simo Zaric and Miroslav Tadic together?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And please tell the Court that.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was very noticeable to me that soldiers would greet them [as interpreted]. When they would see him, they would greet him, because it was obvious that he was occupying a high position. He was the commander of the 4th Detachment. So they would say hello when they saw him, just as they did Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, I wonder whether I could just ask for a clarification from the witness. Page 77, line 9, the witness has said, concerning Mr. Tadic, that he resembled General Draza Mihajlovic from World War II. I'm afraid I don't know how the General looked, and I'm wondering whether you might elaborate a little bit as to what meaning that has for me, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry. I was going to ask, but I thought Mr. Donia covered that, but maybe I'm wrong. Okay. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you just elaborate on who the General was and the significance of the General, please.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that Your Honour didn't know what this General looked like. Serbs know about him. They know about him because his army used to perform killings during World War II. Mr. Tadic was identical to him because he wore a longer beard, because before he used to have a mustache, he had longer hair and he wore round-framed glasses. So he practically resembled General Draza Mihajlovic. All he needed was that cap, the sajkaca, to look exactly like him. And he looked like this throughout the war right up until the exchange. That is what he wore and what he looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did the general wear what they referred to as the Chetnik beard, the big, full beard? Is that what you're describing?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And I believe -- was he the leader of the Chetniks or a major member of the Chetniks, this general?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That general was the number one leader of the Chetnik formations in World War II. And if I may add, I see that he is important to them because in -- throughout the present Republika Srpska, they erected monuments to him, as well as in Brcko. Before, we used to have monuments to heroes from World War II, who were killed in the Partisans, and these were the heroes we were taught about at school. We all know who General Draza was. He was a Chetnik leader. So I understand now that there is a monument to him in Brcko, a Bosnian town, and perhaps in other towns in Bosnia as well. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Just one more question on Miroslav Tadic and Simo Zaric. How were they treated by the officers, the police officers, the military officers, the guards, when they saw either of them?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were generally respectful, or they commanded respect. And when I was in the army I knew what it meant to be an officer, a commander. He would be greeted in a soldier's way. And the only thing that I noticed in the paramilitary soldiers' formations was that the way they greeted or saluted their superiors, and their other conduct was not in accordance with the behaviour of a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were Miroslav Tadic or Simo Zaric saluted when police or local 4th Detachment officers saw them?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And if I may be permitted to add, since I knew both of them, Mr. Simo -- Simic [sic] a little more than Mr. Tadic, because often, as I've already said, I would go with my uncle, I would go hunting with him, so I would often meet Mr. Simo. And each time that I would meet him, I would look at him straight in the eyes so that he would recognise me and perhaps grant me some kind of privileged treatment, but he never seemed to recognise me at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You referred to Mr. Simo and Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm straightening that out.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you referring to Mr. Simo Zaric?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Simo Zaric. I apologise if I made a mistake, but I meant Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when you say you tried to get him to recognise you, were you referring to when you were out on your work assignments or your forced labour assignments?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, outside and inside the police building. Every time I would see -- to see if he would look at me, but he would never look at me because I was unimportant at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: May the witness be shown Exhibit 14A, photograph number 56, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dagovic, do you recognise what's depicted in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Please tell us what is depicted in that photograph.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see the yard of the police station or the detention camp, and you can see here the garages where the prisoners were kept, where the petrol was kept. My uncle was killed in this garage. I was in this garage. And the inmate called Bjelko was in this garage. [redacted] Dragan Lukac and the others were in this garage. This is where we worked. This photograph was taken from a window on the first floor, somewhere here, but you can't see it on this photograph, it was the entrance to the police station. This here is a bunker which we built.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How many garages were there?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I see, it's five, and as I know, it's five, one, two, three, four, five, but I see that the numbers were different. We called them by different numbers when we were in the camp. They went from the other side, because these numbers were not on the doors of the garage at the time that I was in -- detained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let me take you through these five garages. Let's start at the garage which is closest to the bottom of the picture, which appears to be garage 5. You called that garage 1, you referred to that, the prisoners actually --

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What was in garage 1? Please actually point out what you consider garage 1 and then tell us what was in it.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's exactly as we said. We called it garage 1. There was an old car in that garage, from the former police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Garage 2, could you show us where that is and what number is depicted on that now, please?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is now number 4, but before we used to call it number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Who or what was in that garage?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I have to go back a little. When Lugar beat me, [redacted], Dragan Lukac was there, and also a couple of other inmates were there in that garage. I can't remember their names. Franjo Barukcic, because I know that I used to take food to them in that garage. So that's this garage, garage 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What was in the middle garage, garage 3? I assume that one never changed numbers.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were held in that garage. I was kept in that garage, the so-called forced labour group, work group.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you recall anyone else who was ever in that garage?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was there, Antica Bauman was there, Sabah Seric was there, Zlatko Stanic was there. And Enes, he was a mechanic. I don't remember his last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Garage 4, which appears to be depicted as number 2 on the photograph, tell us about that. Who or what was in that garage?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would often unload the stolen goods in that garage, and the police officers used to bring their own stolen goods, their loot, to that garage, and the loot would stay in that garage until they took it home. What I mean to say is that for as long as somebody was on duty, for as long as they worked, as long as they were there, they would steal something and bring it there and then, once they went home, they would take it with them. In that garage, also, my uncle was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We'll get to that shortly. Were there any prisoners held in that garage 4?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And the last one, number 5, which seems to be numbered in the photograph as number 1.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Garage 1 was where petrol was kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Leave that with him for a while and let him talk about it.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So petrol was kept in garage 1. We always had to pour that petrol into all of these cars that you see here, as well as the cars that would -- the cars of the officials who would come to see Mr. Blagoje Simic, so then they would drop by and then we would fill up those cars with petrol as well. I also would like to add: What you see here, this other building, that's already a part of the municipal building. The municipal building was in front, and that's where Mr. Blagoje Simic was, and most probably Mr. Blagoje Simic as well [as interpreted] -- Mr. Milan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the record, the witness is pointing at the building which has windows. It's white and it's situated behind the garage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: He's referring to that as a wing of the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, are you familiar with a man by the name of Ahmed Vukovic?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ahmed Vukovic, yes. That's my uncle. He's my mother's brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And can you tell me whether he was detained with you?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, he was kept in the SUP rooms, but he was also in -- sometimes in garage 3 with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what happened to him, what, if anything, occurred to him?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 28th of November, the police station, or the camp, was shelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. One second. You said 28th of November?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. October. On the 28th of October. I apologise. So we were in this part, in this yard, and we were working on these cars here. Here on the right side, there were two concrete blocks, and this is where we drove the cars onto so that the car would be raised above ground so we could work underneath, and that's where the shelling started. At that moment I happened to be by the door, at the entrance. In view of the fact that the VBR - which is a weapon - when fired, it's very fast, and we could hear it being fired and we could hear the grenades landing. It's a multiple rocket launcher. So I managed to escape closer to the building. My uncle happened to be in garage 4. He was working on something in that garage. The shell landed on the roof of that garage.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what happened to your uncle when the shell landed?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And could you describe his appearance from being shelled?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I sawdust and smoke rising up, but when it subsided, we went out, and one of the detainees, named Hamid -- I don't know what his last name was. He was also known as Conta, Hamid Conta - pulled my uncle's body out. And as far as I was able to see, the right part of his head was missing, a part of his skull on the right side was missing, his hands were all cut up, and so were his legs, his arms. He was giving signs of life, but I think it was just his dying nerves.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was anyone else killed there from shelling prior to your leaving on November 5th?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that in the TO building, a man they called Mrgud was also killed. I don't remember the exact date, but I do know that they shelled that camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was that after your uncle had died or prior to that?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was after my uncle was killed. If I may -- if you will allow me, I would like to add a detail which sticks in my mind. As I said, this garage number 4 was a warehouse for stolen goods, and before the shelling, Pero, that same Pero Krstanovic who took me to loot, as I described this morning, he put some lamps in here that he had stolen somewhere - I don't know where - and after the shelling, they all came here. When I say "they," I'm referring to the soldiers and the police officers. They came to see what had happened here. And Pero said he regretted his lamps, and he didn't pay any attention to the man who was killed here. That's how much a Muslim's life meant to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you indicated there was a bunker in that yard.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How long had that bunker been there?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we built it, I think -- no. I know for certain after I left the hospital we built it. They brought us blocks of concrete and we erected it. That's the bunker. And there was an opening on the front side through which they fired shots at Croatia. You see, this is the river Sava, and the trees here, that's Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I was just going to ask you how it was used. Was the bunker being used prior to your uncle being killed?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And can you explain again how it was being used?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know how? They fired shots from this bunker, not so often, but they did. They fired shots at Croatia, and every time they did, the fire was returned. So that it wasn't just the shelling, but once they fired at the police station - that's this part here - with a anti-aircraft gun, referred to as a PAT. And I was in the toilet at the time, and they shot at the toilet window, and this was probably caused by the provocation by the shots fired by these soldiers and policemen at Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, while you were there in those garages, were there any other dead bodies removed from those garages?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Tell the Court about that, please.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to correct you. This was when I was in the SUP building, but the bodies were taken from the garages, the garage 5, which was then actually number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Please tell us about that, that situation.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So we were in the last room on the right-hand side, and the window of our room was almost at a level with the garage roof. And what we noticed was that there was an unpleasant odour, a stench. We didn't know what it was. But one night we heard a truck arriving. It entered the yard of the police station. The gate was there, and it came up to here. We dared not look out of the window. We heard voices, and we heard something, a thudding on the bottom of the truck. They were probably loading corpses in. And I know that when the truck left, the stench could no longer be smelled. And I did see blood in that garage.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear what happened to those bodies?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but -- well, yes. Later on I did find out that they had Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. buried those bodies in the woods, but I didn't know that then. I hadn't heard that while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And do you know whether those were prisoners, or do you know who that was?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you indicated you were exchanged in early November, on the 5th?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, in the six months that you were held, from May 5th to November 5th, while at the police station, were you ever able to bathe?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the police station, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When I say "the police station," I mean the police station or the garages.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Here in the corner, we used to gather rain water when it rained, and there was an old car there, and behind that car we would bathe quickly so as not to be seen by anyone. I wouldn't call it bathing. It was just sort of perfunctory washing. But in principle, we were not allowed to wash or bathe. And these people in these rooms here, they did not bathe or wash at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What about shaving? Were you able to shave?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What was the condition of your clothing?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my clothing, let me tell you, was very filthy and bloody to begin with, but later on, the good guards would give me a T-shirt or a piece of clothing which I would put on, and then I was able to change and I would throw away what I was able to take off, because it was all bloody and filthy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you allowed to use the bathroom whenever you wanted?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could we talk about the food? You were the person distributing the food. Were you given sufficient amount of food?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How much weight did you lose, if you know, during those six months?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, 15 kilograms, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Can you describe what you were given or how you were fed, the amount of food?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning, I want to say, when I was detained, we were given the food that was brought in by Mr. Tadic's brother, and this was leftovers from the soldiers' meals. I know that for certain because I would get a piece of meat that had been started by someone else. But it was wonderful food compared to what we got later on. This went on until I went to hospital. After I was in hospital, they reduced these rations so that the detainees in the police station and in the garages, the food we got from Tadic's brother or from the police would amount to about three kilograms of bread and one jar of jam, big jam jar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was that three kilograms and jam for one person?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, unfortunately not. This was for all the detainees in the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And about how many detainees shared those three kilograms of bread?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my estimation, there were about 80 prisoners altogether, because there were 49 in my room alone when I was here in the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you hungry while you were being held?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Or I wouldn't have lost so much weight.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: While you were being held at the police station or the garages, were you or the other prisoners beaten?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: With what were you beaten with?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said this morning, I will show you, the door of garage 4 kept opening on its own, so they kept an old car part here, and all the metal tools that were there, all these objects were used to beat us. I will never forget these things. And they beat us very brutally.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Who did the beatings?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly the special soldiers from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Mostly. Who else did the beatings, in addition to the specials from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stevan Todorovic did that often. His escort, his last name was Ristic, I think his first name was Goran. Sometimes people we didn't know, they weren't specials. I could tell they were from our parts by their dialects, they were wearing camouflage uniforms, they would come, they were drunk. So anyone who came in could do what he wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You indicated -- while we are talking about the police, you indicated sometime earlier today that you used to have to clean the police station, clean the corridors, the hallways. What were you cleaning in those corridors and hallways?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
