utterances.text: Well, it was mostly blood, which we had to remove. We also cleaned when there was no blood, but they always gave us something to do. Sometimes we washed blood off walls or doors. We had to take out broken chairs. They broke the chairs while beating us with them. And let me show you in this corner here, this is where we put away those broken chairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's the corner right by the bunker, the area right by the bunker?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, around here. But in this photograph, you can't see, there is another part here, all the way in the corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: During those five months that you spent at the police station, if we subtract the one month from the hospital, how often were people beaten?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People were beaten daily.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: While you were at the police station, were you ever interrogated?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How many times were you interrogated while at the police station?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Who interrogated you, sir?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time, I was interrogated by Mr. Vlado Sarkanovic. Before the war, he was a police inspector. The other two times, it was Milos Savic, also a police inspector before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you describe your condition during these interrogations, your physical condition?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in a very bad state, just like everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Had you been beaten prior to these interrogations?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the interrogations, I myself was never beaten. But before -- I have made connections now in my mind, why did they interrogate us three times? Every time they took me upstairs, of course, I did not admit to what they wanted and then they would take me back and beat me. And then they would call me up again, a few days later, thinking I had changed my mind and I would tell them something. And that's how it went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: During these interrogations, did you write a statement? Did someone take a statement from you? Please describe the process of these interrogations to the Court.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interrogation process went something like this. They told me what I had done. They said, "You were here and you did this and that." For example, they said I was in the SDA military formations, that I had fired shots at Serbs, that -- I don't know, that they had information about me, and I had to sign this. I signed everything they gave me, but they never read it to me, nor did I ever read exactly what I had signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever ask them if you could read the document?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't dare ask them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were these statements that you made, was it voluntary at all?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, no, they weren't. Nothing was voluntary in the camp. Everything was under coercion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when they told you to sign them even though you had not read them, did you sign those statements?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let us just finish up with the police station. While at the police station, did you ever see a man named Stevan Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How often did you see Stevan Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Almost every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you know what his position was at the station?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the chief of police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What was he doing when you saw him on these many days?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every time I saw him, he was maltreating people, beating people, either in passing as he entered the police station and climbed upstairs where his office was. He beat people even then, even if it was only a slap.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see him with any other police officers?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what was he doing with the other police officers?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, mostly when he was maltreating people, the others would laugh and they would strike a few blows.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Have you ever seen -- did you ever see the defendant Simo Zaric at the police station during your five month stay there?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How many times did you see the defendant Simo Zaric at the police station during your five month stay at the station?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 50 times at least, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: On these 50 or so times, or approximately 50 times that you saw him, how was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was wearing a camouflage uniform, which was slightly different from the camouflage uniforms worn by other soldiers, because his uniform was a little lighter in colour. It was more light green while others were of a darker shade of green. Whether it's because he had a high rank or whether it was by accident, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Was he armed when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How was he armed?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He carried an automatic pistol known as a scorpion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see him with any other objects?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what did you see him with?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On his right shoulder he always carried a bag, so the strap would always be on his shoulder, and it was about 30 by 40, or 20 by 30 centimetres in size. I assume he carried important documents in there. I don't know what else he could have carried in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So a briefcase type of a bag?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't -- yes, perhaps. Perhaps a briefcase. In any case, it was a bag for carrying sheets of paper. I had been in the army, and I know that this sort of bag was always carried by officers, and it always contained papers or documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When you saw Simo Zaric, the defendant Simo Zaric, at the police station, what was he usually doing?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. Simo Zaric, as far as I know, ever [as interpreted] hit anyone there, but he would always go upstairs, where the office of Stevan Todorovic was. He probably had meetings with Stevan Todorovic. But I heard when I was in the camp that Mr. Zaric himself interrogated some people in the police station, that is, in the camp. He didn't interrogate me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see Simo Zaric meeting with any of the police officials?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him. Todorovic would sometimes meet him on the stairs. Sometimes they would come down the stairs together. But I mostly saw him with Todorovic, and sometimes with Cancarevic, who was the commander of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You indicated that you were exchanged in early November, on November 5th. Could you tell the Court the circumstances of that exchange, please.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They arrived and they told me I was going to be exchanged, and of course I was happy that I would be able to leave that hell. They took us, five of us detainees, from the police. They took us in the direction of the secondary school, or rather, the sports field near the secondary school. Some buses came there, and we were supposed to board those buses. They were very long buses. We used to refer to them as harmonicas [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Why did you refer to those buses as harmonicas?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Accordians. Because they were double, and in the middle they were connected with a rubber material which was flexible. They were very long buses, maybe 18 metres or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, while you were at the high school waiting as these buses arrived, did you see any of the defendants?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Who did you see?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, Miroslav Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What was the defendant Miroslav Tadic doing?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miroslav Tadic turned up with sheets of paper in his hand, and Tadic and the policeman called out people's names, and as they read out their names, they would board the buses. I wish only to add that there was another camp in the secondary school, and the people from that camp were also boarding the buses. There were lots of civilians, women, and children. Mr. Tadic read out names, and that's the order in which they boarded buses. His assistant was Sreto. I don't know what his last name was, but he was a teacher.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Once you boarded the buses, what happened next?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then we set out toward Crkvina, and we stopped in the village of Zasevica. That's where the next camp was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what happened there?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that occasion a few women and children and elderly men were brought onto the bus, and then we continued on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Where did you go from there?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went in the direction of Doboj, Derventa, Banja Luka, and then we turned toward Nova Gradiska.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What happened at Gradiska?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may add, if you will allow me: During the journey there, there was a Serbian checkpoint every two or three kilometres, and they always stopped the bus. Of course, they knew that we were going to be exchanged, that we were civilians, but they wanted to kill us all. However, on one occasion I noticed Sreto saying, "Don't kill them. We'll get Serbs in exchange for them." Then we got to Gradiska. Mr. Tadic was driving in a car, a civilian vehicle, in front, and there was another car which was a police car. I remember well that we stopped in Gradiska, in front of the bridge, that is, in front of the border with Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How long did you sit in that bus in Gradiska by the bridge?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did you see Miroslav Tadic at that time?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic went to a cafe which was near the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: During those two hours, were you allowed to leave the bus, you and the other people?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we were not allowed to do so; and even had we done so, it would not have ended well for us, because the people from Gradiska wanted to kill us. Across the road there was a school, and the students came out and hurled insults at us. So we were actually fortunate to be in the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Where did you go next?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When, as they say, they put the papers in order, we crossed over into Croatia, and right after we had crossed the bridge, we were stopped by Martic's police, the police of Milan Martic. They looked at the documents and the list of names, and they asked if anyone had any gold jewellery to hand over. I don't know whether people did that. I didn't have anything with me. I was just out of camp. I don't know whether other people had something to give and what they took. When this was over, we went on our way toward Dragalic, about 15 to 20 kilometres away, and we came to an abandoned petrol pump which I think had been burnt, and there we were exchanged through the mediation of the Nepal battalion of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In what country did this occur?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And at this time during the exchange, were any of the defendants present?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Who was present?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Miroslav Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what was he doing?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had papers in his hand again, and some man came from the other side and they agreed on something, and that's how the exchange started.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And can you just explain what the exchange looked like?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The exchange looked like this: I think on one side, I think Mr. Tadic went to the place where the bus was, the bus in which the Serb prisoners came; and the other one, the representative of the other side, came to our side, and he read from a list, and we were to cross over to the other side. And Mr. Tadic or someone else probably read the list on the other side for those people to cross over. And then we got into a bus in which the Serb prisoners were brought, and they got into the bus in which we were brought. What I noticed was the following: I was glad that this other bus was much more luxurious than the bus that I was brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And where did you go in this newer bus, on this luxurious bus?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were taken to Orasje on this new bus. Orasje is in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What happened once you got to Orasje?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived at Orasje, the first thing I did was to take a bath and to eat well. Since it was already night, we went to sleep, to some houses that were there, to the headquarters. I don't know what they called it. And then the next day I went for a medical examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let us talk about your medical status. What injuries did you suffer while being imprisoned in Bosanski Samac, at the police station?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The injuries that I sustained are broken ribs, extracted teeth, broken fingers, the cutting of my ears and my neck, the cutting of my fingers, abuse, blows and pains that I still feel when there is about to be a change in the weather. And the worst is that I still have psychological problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you please describe some of the psychological problems that you've suffered and maybe still are suffering?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My psychological problems are depression, stress, hyperventilation, problems with my muscles. The problems with my muscles are a result of tension, and then they are related to other problems, problems with my bladder and other organs as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Tell me about the problems with the muscles, please. Tell the Court.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The problems with my muscles? Well, if I were to tell you that I had 20 treatments with my doctor where I go regularly for massages of my muscles, because those muscles are pressing upon the blood vessels in the back of my neck, so I have weak concentration, I get upset very easily, I sleep badly because of that, I get headaches, I have problems with my bladder. And I have undertaken all the medical tests in Holland, and I have medical -- documentation about this. Because of the muscle tension, there is pressure on my bladder so that I cannot have control over my bladder. The control over my bladder has been taken over by stress, which also affects my other organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did these problems exist prior to your being incarcerated in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. I never even had to go and see a doctor, except when I was a child and had to be vaccinated. Now I have a very thick medical file with my GP, and also at the clinics in my town. And I can also tell you, and I can document that, that 20 days ago, I ended up in the emergency room precisely because I had an irregular heartbeat, hyperventilation, vertigo, and all of this is a consequence of the stress.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What about dental work? You indicated you had four of your teeth pulled by Lugar. Did you have any dental work done after you got out of the prison at the police station?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received permission to leave Bosnia and Herzegovina, to leave the area of Orasje. I was permitted to go to Croatia. Since I had friends in Istria in Croatia, I went to Novi Grad, where I had my teeth repaired. I had dentures made.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you have any problems with your jaw from the beatings?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My upper jaw is deformed. It's shifted a little to the side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I realise this is not as important as your physical problems, but could we just talk about your financial losses that you suffered, that you and your family suffered? What ever happened to your Ford Capri?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ford Capri was taken, was driven away by Tralja. On that occasion, when he came, they took 17.000 German marks from our house. They took my mother's gold jewellery. And they took valuable items which they were able to carry, smaller items.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When you say "they," who were "they"?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean Tralja and the people who were with him, mostly the specials, the so-called soldiers from the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What was taken from you? Let's talk about jewellery.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, that time, they took 17 rings from my mother. Since, as I've already said, gold was a tradition in our family, and it would be inherited from one generation to the next, so that we had quite a lot of gold, and they took that away. But this wasn't the only time that they came and took things and jewellery from us. They came several times, on several occasions, and they even fired shots around the house and abused my parents and my brother. And this can be confirmed by a gentleman who is among the accused, if he wishes to do that, because he helped to a certain extent. He helped my parents to a certain extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What else did your family lose?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My family lost just, like all the other families lost, a house. I have to go back a little. I have to come back to the present. As I said, we had two houses, so they took both of those houses. So when we were exchanged, this was left behind automatically, and other refugees moved into our houses and they took all our things. Now, the house that my uncle lived in, my father's brother, for that house, they made some sort of false documents, some kind of contract, which is -- claims that this was given as a gift, which is absolutely not true. So we had to go to court over this house. This has happened over the past year. I must say that one of the lawyers on the other side was a lawyer who was in the team of these gentlemen here. He's very popular over there, and I'm very unpopular over there, because I am a witness in The Hague, and this was the reason why I definitely lost the house, to which I have all the deeds. This house is wholly owned by my father and this is the only reason. So that means I have come to the conclusion with this that they had rounded off their ethnic cleansing by doing this. They expelled us, they are -- they placed the house in the name of a man from Obudovac, the house for which I have all the documents, which I can produce here in The Hague. Yesterday when I was here in The Hague, when I went to a break, my lawyer called me from Samac and he told me that the Court of Republika Srpska has rejected our appeal to the basic court in Doboj, on the decision of the basic court in Doboj, which awarded the house to them. So that means that the circle of ethnic cleansing has this way been completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Before I ask you a few questions on that, you indicated that somebody in this courtroom was aware of one of the problems and helped your family. Could you tell us who that was and what that's about, please?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that occasion, when the soldiers from Serbia came, when they abused my parents, when they forced them -- excuse me, when they forced my brother and my father to drink in one go one litre of whiskey all at once, meaning that they could not stop, that they beat them, abused them, they fired weapons in the house, and my parents, the only thing that they had -- could do, after -- those soldiers left and they said they were going to come back in half an hour, so my parents set out towards the house of my aunt, which is my grandfather's house, the house where my father was born. Since this was close to the place where Mr. Borislav Pisarevic lived, he saw my parents, and he knew them well and they knew him well, too, so he helped them in the sense that he came up to help them, he gave them some water, he asked them what had happened, and then my mother told him what happened, and he probably, if he remembers that, he could see what a state they were in. I hope he does remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. This house that you were talking about that you lost, or that you're involved in litigation with at this time, was this -- for how many generations was this house in your family?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four generations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In whose name is this house registered?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The house was registered in the name of my mother, or my great-grandmother, who gave that house to my uncle, my father's brother, who died in 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: As of April of 1992, in whose name is that house registered?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The house was registered in the name of my uncle, Sulejman Dagovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: After your uncle died, in whose name was it registered?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After my uncle died in 1999, I personally went to Samac with my father, and again, on that occasion I saw Mr. Pisarevic, and I asked for his advice, since he's a lawyer, what I should do, so that we should register the house in my father's name. If he remembers, he sent me to the municipality, told me to take out a death certificate. Then they sent me to Doboj, where he died. I got the certificate of death from there, and based on that I went to the courthouse with my father, where it was established that there was no will and testament, that there was no contract giving the house as a gift. There was no document at all with which my uncle, who died in 1997, had left this house to anybody else, which means that my father is the only legal inheritor who would have that house. And based on that, we registered the house in my father's name, and I have all of those documents here in Holland. If I may continue, if you allow me, maybe two months ago, or perhaps a little more, I received a telephone call from Obudovac. This is a village near Samac. And a man asked me during the call whether I was interested in selling the house. I asked, "Which house, sir?" I asked him, "The one in front and the one behind," because both houses were in our name. And he said that he bought the one in the front and he was now interested in the one in the back. And I asked, "How could you have bought that house when the house is registered in our name?" He told me that he had bought it, he had registered it over to his name and that everything was okay. I called Milos Savic, who interrogated me in the camp in 1992, in view of the fact that he works in the Court where all of those documents are kept, and I asked him if he could check for me who is -- in whose name is the house registered. And he gave me information that the house is in the name of Sarkanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the first name.

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A man from Obudovac, together with my father I engaged a lawyer, who then set out to work to see what this whole thing was about. They showed us a contract where there is a signature which is not my uncle's signature, and they said that this house was left to this man by contract. So all of the gentlemen sitting here are versed in the law, and they know very well the procedure when a house is registered in somebody's name. So if there is a contract, this contract must be at court. So when we tried to register the house and we did in our name, there was no such contract. And if there had been, we would have known about it. So then we had to prove that we were caring for our brother, my uncle, my father's brother, and that throughout the war we sent money, and that I had received papers from the Dutch ministry for him to be able to come here, and that once he died, we buried him and we erected him -- had a gravestone made for him. And the only reason why Mr. Zivan -- and the only reason for this whole affair perhaps is that is Mr. Zivan Blagojevic, who is also here in The Hague, is very popular, and I, who am also in The Hague, am not very popular. Yesterday I heard that they had a small celebration because they had completed their job.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When you say that there was a contract but it did not have your uncle's signature, are you saying it was a forged signature, or was the signature of someone other than your uncle, meaning there's a different name on that piece of paper granting title?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that it's a forged signature, because I have letters and signatures and documents by my uncle which all bear his signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, there was a name, this very house in which the name was registered, Mr. Sarkanovic. The interpreters said that they didn't get the first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What was the first name of that individual named Sarkanovic, from Obudovac, who claims to own the house now?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slobodan Sarkanovic. If you wanted to put things together. But I did inform myself, and I know that Sarkanovic is a cousin of the interrogator who interrogated me in the camp. They are in power down there. They are everything down there. And if you permit me, we also have to pay for all the court expenses, and including the lawyers. These expenses amount to about 20.000 German marks. If we do not do that, they - and I have this in writing - they will carry out measures. And since I do not intend to make this payment, they probably intend to sell my house in order to complete this cycle of ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You were speaking about your uncle's house, the house that's been in your family for four generations, and you claim it's been -- you're losing it through fraud. The house in back, the house that your family, your parents were living in, what's the status of that house?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That house is still registered in my father's name. How long this will be for, I have no idea, but it still is in my father's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Has anyone been living in either of these houses since 1992, other than your family?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When we were expelled, Serb refugees moved in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Is anyone living there at this time, now nine years later?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until recently, a man from Glamoc lived in my uncle's house. Now he's returned to his own house and now the house has been taken over by this person who has allegedly bought it. My house is inhabited by refugees from Drvar, and I have just received information that they are about to leave. So that I am hoping that I will get my house back, if it's not taken away from me again, in view of what I have just said, because what I have said now, they will already know that tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's start off with your uncle's house. While people were living there, did you ever receive any rent or any money while they were staying there, from those people?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After my uncle died, and after they moved in, nobody has paid anything. They even asked us, when they were leaving, for us to pay them 5.000 German marks so that they would not take everything from our house, all the things from our house. Also, in connection with this house, Judge Momir Djosanovic, who conducted this court proceeding, said that if we gave him 15.000 German marks, that he would take care of everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let us go to the next house, the house that your family was living in. You claim -- you told us -- you've testified that Serb refugees moved in after they forced your family out, and apparently people are going to be leaving soon, some nine years later. During these nine years, did you ever receive any rent or any payment from the people living in that house, from the government, for the use of that house, nine years' use? Have you received any payment?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: With regard to either of the houses, did you ever receive any document indicating that your house has been seized for a certain period for people to stay there?

utterances.speaker: ESAD DAGOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before the cross-examination starts, I just wanted to inform the parties, especially the Defence counsel, the Defence counsels for Mr. Simo Zaric, that cross-examination for the following witnesses – (redacted), Mr. Dagovic; Mr. Omer Nalic; (redacted); Mr. Perica Misic; and Mr. Kemo Mehinovic - will be conducted by co-counsel, Mr. Lazarevic, and perhaps other witnesses as the evidence progresses, because they may not be listed here, but depending on the evidence -- as the evidence goes. After that, I wanted to find out how many counsel will cross-examine the witness. All the counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We believe, Your Honours, that all the counsels will conduct the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Okay. In view of the time, I think we shall adjourn the cross-examination to the week after next week, when we resume our proceedings on the 19th of November, at 0930 hours. So Mr. Dagovic, you have to come on the 19th of November for cross-examination, because next week the Trial Chamber has a recess. Before we rise, is there any other matter? MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, and for the benefit of the Chamber and Defence counsel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: The expected order of witnesses after this witness will be, and in this order: Witness G; [redacted] [redacted]; Perica Misic; (redacted) ; Safet Dagovic; and Ewa Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. And maybe to lessen the confusion, we can have a document which can be served on the parties and the Trial Chamber. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, I will do that. And there is just one other matter relating to variant A and B document. Perhaps it's best that Ms. Reidy addresses you on that, since she prepared the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: It's just that I have with me the witness summary of an investigator who would be the witness we would call should this matter be taken further with the Chamber. And there are some other supporting documentation to that witness summary. So I have copies here for Defence, and obviously for the senior legal officer and the Registry, just so that the Chamber is advised that the Defence can consider the contents of these, the witness statements, that -- during the recess. As they indicated, they may want to make submissions on these files. Is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I want to be clear. You are not going to call the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Well, as indicated before, the witness is not someone who is -- was currently listed on our witness list. This is a witness we will call if the Chamber requires, if the Chamber determines that's the way it should go. If we want this document authenticated, it's best done through a live witness, that's the witness we would call. Or alternatively, since it's not a matter that goes to any of the direct actions of the defendants, it could also be testimony taken by way of 92 bis, I think it is. But this is the witness summary, this is the sort of testimony that the witness would give, should the witness appear, either as -- to give live, viva voce testimony, or to provide it by way of 92 bis. I don't know. I know Your Honour Judge Singh had suggested it may be a way to expedite matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. You can go ahead and distribute the documents. I'm sure the Defence would like to have sufficient time to look at them before they are called upon to make their own submissions. Any matter from the Defence before we rise?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If you permit me, I think this witness can be escorted, because we have some procedural matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: He's probably too tired for -- after the testimony, so probably Mr. Usher can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The usher will escort the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Just one other matter on the issue of the variant A and B document that my colleague Ms. Reidy addressed you on. Of course it's still possible at this stage that the Defence might withdraw their objection, so all this evidence may become moot, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What do you mean? After giving them the documents, you think if they look through -- MR. DI FAZIO: They may withdraw their objection to the admission into evidence of the variant A and B document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Oh, I see what you mean. Yes, yes. MR. DI FAZIO: If that happens, then therefore this is moot, and it may be that there is still hope for that possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Everything is possible in life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic? What matters do you wish to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In response to my learned colleague, I said everything is possible in life, especially in legal proceedings, so probably after the -- I don't know, actually. So maybe, maybe we shall withdraw, maybe we shall rest. Your Honours, I'm not so sure whether I proceed in a formal form, in form of motion, but allow me first to raise the issue, and then you will see whether it will be necessary to have a motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We as a Defence in this case, we have noticed, during the course of these trial proceedings that, to some extent, we think that, during the objection, objections, during the course of proceedings raised by Prosecution, certain formulation might have significant impact to the issue of testimony of particular witness. So I would kindly suggest and ask - I mean, we have a break of seven days, so we all can think about that issue - whether in further proceedings we shall proceed with the practice in a short conference and approach the bench about some procedural matters, or we shall - which I'm not in favour of the second option - that the particular witness in question should be escorted for a few minutes and then brought back during the trial proceedings, which is I think a little bit complicated. The bottom line of this submission is that, as I said, there is certain impression that when the Prosecution, in course of the objection -- procedural objections establishing a foundation for something, that theoretically - and I'm afraid practically - the witness can catch something in the air, a word or issue or topic or whatever. Or whether, a third possibility, the Prosecution will object with the very short notions, such as, let's say -- sorry, repetitive or, you know, other things, without further explanations why it's repetitive. Or we can approach the Bench and clarify these things, because these are strictly Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. procedural matters. And as I said, maybe I'm wrong, but we have some kind of impression. It's just, I would say, topic for thinking. It's not an urgent matter. It's not an issue that we can discuss or resolve now, but it's just an impression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any other matters? That's all? That's all. Thank you. The Court will rise and the proceedings will continue on the 19th of November at 0930 hours.
